thread.title: Intel-Apple Rumor: Bears Mull Existential Risk

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Intel-Apple Rumor: Bears Mull Existential Risk
text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated April 3, 2018 6:23 p.m. ET Illustration: Intel Inc. The Street is mulling the rumor yesterday from Bloomberg that Apple ( AAPL ) will dump Intel ( INTC ) chips from its Mac computers come 2020.
Intel shares defied the negative speculation today, rising by 83 cents, or 1.7%, to close at $49.75.
As I noted yesterday , several people have stepped up to defend Intel. The main point of those bullish on Intel stock is that the rumor’s been around a while, so it must be taken with a grain of salt. And even if it’s true, Apple’s purchases of microprocessors for the Mac amounts to a very small business for Intel, given how little market share Apple has in personal computers.
But a fair number of bears stepped forward today with ominous interpretations.
In the bear argument, the merest whiff of Apple stepping away suggests Apple is pointing to a weakness in Intel’s roadmap for its chips.
Here’s a bit from each of the two camps:
Bullish!
John Pitzer, Credit Suisse: Reiterates an Outperform rating. “The Sky is Falling…Again […] This has been an existential threat ever since AAPL introduced the A4 processor in CY10 for the iPhone, and was first speculated by Bloomberg back in 2012 […] The specificity of the article does lend some credibility. It is clear to us that AAPL has been working towards a goal of 'moving up the stack' if only to keep INTC ‘honest' – but we see the sell-off as an over-reaction […] It is unclear what moving up the stack offers – a unified OS seems tertiary as apps have become more form-factor specific, it would likely open up the risk of performance/compatibility issues, and a move down with a lower cost solution seems antithetical to AAPL’s ‘premium' strategy."
C.J. Muse, Evercore ISI : Reiterates an Outperform rating. "We note that news reports about such a transition have circulated for almost a decade […] While this is clearly a risk to Intel, we believe it is a minor one, as AAPL CPUs likely drive only ~4% of Intel’s revenue (we see worst case EPS impact of $0.15 roughly 5yrs from now, as a transition will not be immediate – and this does not include incremental baseband revenues). So big picture, while we understand investor concerns about the loss of a marquee customer, we note that a) the loss is far from certain; b) a loss would likely be gradual, and c) INTC likely retains AAPL's baseband business. Were Apple to stop using INTC CPUs, it would likely do so gradually, with the final EPS hit likely comprising less than 3% of EPS in the early 2020s – which will likely be more than offset by Intel’s operational improvements and topline growth elsewhere."
Srini Pajjuri, Macquarie: Reiterates an Outperform rating. "While we have no visibility into Apple’s plans, we remain skeptical. We do not foresee ARM-based Macs matching the user experience of those based on Intel x86 CPUs anytime soon (Chromebook market is a good example). We doubt if Apple will consider offering products that will likely be viewed as inferior to comparable Windows PCs. While Apple could look to switch only low-end (MacBook Air) to internal CPUs, that would mean fragmenting the OS and applications (MSFT’s Windows on ARM efforts have had limited success). In the worst case that Apple switches 100% of Macs to internal CPUs, we see ~3% EPS impact for Intel. As such, we are not overly concerned about the speculation."
Bearish!
Hans Mosesmann, Rosenblatt : Reiterates a Sell rating on Intel shares. “Strategic OEMs like Apple have access and unique visibility into silicon ‘roadmaps’ and their peek into Intel’s would perhaps show something that is suspect. If the roadmap was compelling you just wouldn’t make that move, we believe. We do know that Intel’s 14nm process node is long in the tooth by over 2 years and the very late 10nm appears not a volume process until 2019 […] Apple’s potential move also highlights the restrictions and vulnerabilities imposed on Intel CPUs of a decelerating Moore’s Law."
Stacy Rasgon, Bernstein : Reiterates an Underperform rating. "This latest market speculation feels more real. Apple is not a huge PC vendor […] The bigger risk is whether this could simply be, if true, the first crack to the story that could conceivably develop into a chasm. One leg of our bear case on Intel is the presence of renewed competition in markets that were previously effective monopolies, and major customers doing their own silicon is a potentially significant aspect of that. If AAPL can prove that their own architecture (presumably manufactured by other suppliers as Intel's process lead withers) can credibly replace what have likely been high-end SKUs from Intel, an existence proof for the potential viability of ARM in the PC space will have been provided […] What will happen if / when datacenter customers, already beginning to develop their own silicon for specialized workloads, decide that expanding these efforts might make sense?"
Mark Lipacis, Jefferies & Co .: Reiterates an Underperform rating. "The report is not substantiated, but is consistent with 1) our Moore Stress 2.0 thesis that argues that semis would see vertical integration by customers, and 2) our concern that INTC's risk is increased competition and lower margins, even as most semis are benefiting from consolidation-driven pricing power and higher margins."
